column3: Population split into M sub-populations; sub-population m is selected by tournaments on objective m only, then everything is mixed and varied.
column4: • Simplest multiobjective GA: one line changes the selection.; • Very fast (0.0s for 10,000 evaluations) †.; • No ranking, no sorting, no sharing parameters.; • Finds the extreme solutions quickly: 88 points on P2 with IGD 0.013 †.; • Works with any variation operator.
column5: • Collapses to the extremes: a single point (n = 1, HV 0.000) on P3 †.; • On P2 about 96 % of the final points sit in the low-cost half (study) †.; • Middle compromise solutions are mediocre in every single objective, so tournaments never favour them ('speciation').; • No elitism: a good non-dominated set can be lost in the next generation.; • No constraint handling or diversity preservation.

column7: Anything where the compromise region matters.

column3: Rank = 1 + number of dominators; fitness interpolated by rank; fitness sharing in objective space; fitness-proportionate selection.
column4: • Dominance-based, so it finds the middle of the front: P5 n = 57, HV 0.808 †.; • Sharing keeps points spread.; • Conceptually simple, objective-scale-free after min-max.; • No external archive needed.; • Cheap: 0.2s †.
column5: • Non-elitist: on P3 only 25 points, HV 0.386 vs NSGA-II's 0.487 †.; • Sharing radius σ must be tuned; wrong σ gives clusters (Spacing 0.032 on P5 vs NSGA-II 0.011) †.; • Rank-to-fitness mapping and scaling are arbitrary.; • O(N²M) dominance counting.; • Fitness-proportionate selection is sensitive to scaling.
column6: Historical/baseline Pareto-ranking GA on small 2-objective problems.
column7: Hard fronts such as ZDT2 within 10,000 evaluations.

column3: Fronts from non-dominated sorting; front k gets dummy fitness slightly below front k−1's minimum shared fitness; sharing inside each front.
column4: • Strong pressure towards the front through layered fitness; P5 HV 0.802 †.; • Sharing inside each front spreads points.; • Constraints by penalty: 69 points on P5 and 25 on P7 †.; • Natural predecessor of NSGA-II, easy to follow.; • Needs no archive.
column5: • Non-elitist, and on P7 returns only 25 points (HV 0.632) vs 85 points (HV 0.699) for Constrained NSGA-II †.; • O(M N³) sorting and O(N²) sharing – the slowest of the early methods.; • Sharing radius σ must be tuned.; • IGD 0.022 on P5 is worse than NSGA-II's 0.013 †.; • Fitness-proportionate selection is scale sensitive.
column6: Learning the history of Pareto-based GAs.

column3: Binary tournament: both candidates are compared with a random comparison set (10 % of N); a dominated candidate loses; ties go to the smaller niche count.
column4: • No global ranking or sorting – selection cost is O(N·t_dom).; • Selection pressure is tunable through t_dom; P5 HV 0.797 †.; • Niche counts keep diversity.; • Cheap selection without sorting: 0.5s per 10,000 evaluations †.; • Works with any variation operator.
column5: • Weak on P3: HV 0.055, IGD 0.446 after 10,000 evaluations †.; • t_dom too small → almost random selection, too large → premature convergence.; • Needs both t_dom and the niche radius σ.; • Non-elitist.; • Slower than NSGA-II here (0.4s vs 0.4s) †, because of the Python tournament loop.
